newsitem.title: FRANCE: Former Credit Lyonnais head in custody.
newsitem.headline: Former Credit Lyonnais head in custody.

text.p: Jean-Maxime Leveque, who headed state-controlled bank Credit Lyonnais from 1986 to 1988, was taken into custody on Thursday on suspicion of false accounting and complicity to embezzle, judicial sources said.
They said the ex-banker was formally placed under investigation by judge Eva Joly in connection with her probe International Bankers (IBSA), a former subsidiary of Credit Lyonnais, the source said.
Being placed under investigation in France is a preliminary step to a trial but does not imply guilt.

The investigation, launched in 1994 following a complaint by Credit Lyonnais, is focusing on allegations the accounts of IBSA were inflated by about one billion francs ($175 million) during the 1991-92 financial year and that some 10 million francs ($1.75 million) in non-existent dividends were distributed to certain unnamed shareholders.
IBSA became a subsidiary of Credit Lyonnais in 1990.
Leveque, 73, was head of Credit Commercial de France before leading Credit Lyonnais.

IBSA, which was set up by Leveque, now is under the control of state-backed Consortium de realisation, a holding set up by the government in 1995 to sell assets of Credit Lyonnais which almost collapsed in the early 1990s under the weight of earlier lending excesses.
A number of other figures who were involved with IBSA are also being investigated. IBSA's former managing director Gerard Mantelet has also been detained as part of the same inquiry.

Joly is already investigating former subsidiaries of the bank which made some of its most controversial loans during the late 1980s and 1990s. At least 40 judicial inquiries are under way into the activities of the bank's former units.
Joly was also named earlier this year to probe allegations of fraud at the parent bank in a bid to seek those responsible for one of the biggest financial scandals in French banking history.

Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said last year he wanted to bring former senior managers of the parent bank to justice for failing to keep control of subsidiaries during its expansion spree that briefly transformed it into the largest bank outside Japan.
